clue.text: Appearing for trial, drunk is tense

parts.note: someone up before the magistrates is appearing in court to be tried
tight is informal for intoxicated

explanation.surface: A defendant turns up to court drunk and on edge.
explanation.walkthrough: To be 'up' before a court is to appear there for trial.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe someone anxious and on edge, so they are synonyms.

clue.text: Lots consumed by plump teenagers

indicators.note: the answer is eaten up by the two following words, sitting inside them across the gap

explanation.surface: Large quantities of food get eaten by chubby adolescents.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal word for a great many, an indefinitely large number.

clue.text: Fetch over boy all treated as an arrogant know-all?

definitions.note: the phrase describes such a person; the question mark admits the definition is by description rather than a strict synonym

indicators.note: letters that are treated are processed or worked on, so the four words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Telling a boy to fetch things is how you treat a smug show-off.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a description: the answer is the adjective you would apply to an arrogant know-all.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes someone so pleased with their own cleverness that they become irritating.

clue.text: Expression used when turning in honourable noble that's abandoned king

parts.note: an honourable person is good

indicators.note: the noble has given up the letter for king, so it is dropped

parts.note: a knight is a titled member of the nobility in a loose sense
K is the chess and card abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: An upright aristocrat who has deserted his monarch, rendered as a bedtime farewell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turning in' means going to bed, not turning someone over to the authorities.
explanation.definitionFit: The farewell people say on retiring to bed for the night.

clue.text: Implied historian not with us

indicators.note: the historian's name is taken without the following word, so those letters go

parts.note: Tacitus was a Roman historian
taken as written

explanation.surface: A historian who disagrees with us has been hinted at rather than stated.
explanation.definitionFit: Something implied is understood without being stated, which is exactly what unspoken agreement means.

clue.text: Called up, composed

explanation.definitionFit: One word covers being conscripted for military service and having written a first version of a document.

clue.text: Get rid of bugs in den, if it's terribly cold inside

indicators.note: the abbreviation for cold goes inside the rearranged letters
terribly suggests the words are badly messed up, so their letters are rearranged

parts.note: C is the standard abbreviation for cold, as on taps

explanation.surface: Insects infest a lair, so someone fumigates it, though it is bitterly cold inside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'terribly' turns DEN IF ITS into DISINFET, and 'inside' puts C into it.
explanation.definitionFit: To clean with chemicals so that germs are killed; bugs here are microbes.

clue.text: On one's own in plant, bottling nitrogen

indicators.note: the plant holds the element in, as a bottle holds liquid

parts.note: aloe is a succulent plant
N is the chemical symbol for nitrogen

explanation.surface: Someone alone in a factory, bottling a gas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plant' suggests a factory, but it is the succulent.
explanation.definitionFit: Being by oneself, without company, is a direct synonym.

clue.text: Assumes fan, streaker, got excited close to end

indicators.note: excited suggests agitation, so the three words are stirred up and rearranged
the close of a word is its final letter

explanation.surface: A sports fan and a streaker got worked up as the match neared its finish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'excited' rearranges FAN STREAKER GOT into TAKESFORGRANTE, and 'close to' takes the final D of 'end'.
explanation.definitionFit: To accept something as true without question is to assume it.

clue.text: Daughter on railway on headland shows sign of thirst

parts.note: D is the abbreviation for daughter in genealogy
a ness is a promontory, as in Loch Ness place names

explanation.surface: A girl perched on a railway line on a cliff top displays a parched look.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' means placed above, so the pieces stack in order.
explanation.definitionFit: Lack of moisture in the mouth is a symptom of being thirsty.

clue.text: Process, in my book, confused a primate

indicators.note: confused means mixed up, so the letters of the words are jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone finds a procedure baffling, by their reckoning.
explanation.definitionFit: This long-nosed Borneo monkey is an example of a primate.

clue.text: Bit of theatre'll entertain this woman

indicators.note: only a portion of the phrase is used, the letters spanning the word gap

explanation.surface: Part of the theatre will amuse a particular lady.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's first name, so the clue points at a particular female person.

clue.text: Indefinite number diving in seen struggling in Tees, swirling river

indicators.note: the whole inner group goes inside the second jumbled word
swirling water churns things around, so the river's letters are rearranged
the number plunges into the middle of the jumbled word
struggling suggests thrashing about, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: N stands for an unspecified number in mathematics

explanation.surface: Someone seen diving and struggling in the swirling waters of the Tees, an English river.
explanation.walkthrough: Two layers of insertion: the jumbled 'seen' with its N sits between the first letter and the rest of the jumbled 'Tees'. 'river' looks like part of the surface scene but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A major American river, flowing through the state of the same name, is an example of a river.

clue.text: Easy to get around in one, vehicle brought back by bishop in storm

indicators.note: brought back means turned round, so the word reads backwards

parts.note: a van is a road vehicle
I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: the bishop's letter is placed within the storm

parts.note: a gale is a strong storm wind
B is the chess notation abbreviation for bishop

explanation.surface: A bishop drives a van back through a storm to show the roads are passable.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition swallows the first 'in'; it is not a container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A waterway that boats can travel along is one that is easy to get around in.

clue.text: Head for Bertie's on arrival, then southern seat of Lord Emsworth

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

parts.note: a landing is the arrival of an aircraft

explanation.surface: Bertie heads for a southern stately home, a nod to Wodehouse's Bertie Wooster.
explanation.walkthrough: Blandings Castle is Lord Emsworth's country house in P G Wodehouse's novels; Bertie Wooster is another Wodehouse hero, adding to the scene.
explanation.definitionFit: In Wodehouse's fiction the castle of this name is the ancestral home of the earl.

clue.text: Female fatality in Eliot's river

parts.note: a death is a loss of life

explanation.surface: A woman dies in a river from a George Eliot novel.
explanation.walkthrough: George Eliot wrote 'The Mill on the Floss', whose heroine drowns in the river.
explanation.definitionFit: The river of George Eliot's novel title, in which her heroine Maggie Tulliver dies.

clue.text: Sample speciality — about to indulge to the full when served up

indicators.note: the speciality wraps around the other piece

parts.note: one's forte is what one does best

indicators.note: in a down entry, served up means presented upwards, so the word reads backwards

parts.note: to sate is to satisfy an appetite fully

explanation.surface: A chef's signature dish, about to be served so diners can eat their fill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about to' reads as 'on the point of', but 'about' is the container signal and 'to' a link; 'served up' only works because this is a down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A foretaste is a small early sample of something to come.

clue.text: Slight quarrel about river fish

indicators.note: the quarrel goes around the letter for river

parts.note: a spat is a petty argument
R is the map abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: A minor tiff over a fish caught in a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'river fish' reads as one phrase, but the river supplies R and 'fish' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A small sea creature of the herring family, so an example of a fish.

clue.text: Member in rear, mostly, in race

indicators.note: the limb is set inside the shortened word
mostly means all but the last letter is kept

parts.note: the stern is the rear of a ship
a leg is a limb, a member of the body

explanation.surface: A limb mostly at the back during a race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' turns STERN into STER, and 'in' puts LEG into it. The St Leger is a classic British horse race run at Doncaster.
explanation.definitionFit: A famous annual flat horse race in England, the oldest of the five Classics.

clue.text: Very close friends, for example, love changes externally

indicators.note: the changes sit on the outside, around the other pieces

parts.note: to alter is to change
love is zero in tennis, shaped like the letter O

explanation.surface: Love, for instance, changes on the outside.
explanation.definitionFit: A second self, an intimate friend who is like another version of oneself.

clue.text: Bad language — not good to admit to office

indicators.note: the letter for good is not included, so it is removed

parts.note: swearing is bad language

explanation.surface: Foul language is no good for someone being admitted to office.
explanation.definitionFit: Formally installing someone in a role by having them take an oath of office.

clue.text: Editorial about Scottish town preacher

indicators.note: the editorial wraps around the town

parts.note: a leader is a newspaper's leading article or editorial
Ayr is a town on Scotland's west coast

explanation.surface: A newspaper editorial about a preacher from a Scottish town.
explanation.definitionFit: A lay reader is an unordained person licensed to lead services and preach in the Church of England.

clue.text: Embarrassed, the Parisian put up senior church member

indicators.note: in a down entry, put up means raised, so the letters read upwards

parts.note: embarrassed people go red
le is French for the

explanation.surface: A red-faced Frenchman is promoted to church office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put up' reverses RED LE, giving the letters read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: In Presbyterian churches an elder is an officer who helps govern the congregation.

clue.text: Plump? Here's a single slice of bread!

definitions.meaning: one slice of bread, or a sandwich made from it

explanation.definitionFit: One word means both rotund in shape and, in British usage, a slice of bread.

clue.text: Find stock after short time

indicators.note: the word for stock comes after the letter for time

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for time
stock means lineage or race

explanation.surface: Locating inventory after a brief wait.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stock' suggests goods in a shop, but here it is ancestry.
explanation.definitionFit: To trace someone or something is to track it down and locate it.

clue.text: Missing trick, conquistador in ring upset Torquemada, perhaps

indicators.note: upset means knocked over and disordered, so the letters are rearranged
the word for trick goes missing from the explorer's title

parts.note: a con is a trick or swindle

explanation.surface: A Spanish conquistador, missing a trick, is upset by the chief inquisitor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Missing' takes CON from CONQUISTADOR, leaving QUISTADOR; 'upset' rearranges that with IN RING.
explanation.definitionFit: Tomás de Torquemada was the first head of the Spanish Inquisition, an example of this title.

clue.text: Makes alterations to Religious Education classes

parts.note: RE is the school subject abbreviation
forms are school classes in British schools

explanation.surface: A school changes how its Religious Education classes are run.
explanation.definitionFit: To reform something is to change and improve it.

clue.text: Needs to be treated by doctor in a city in Saxony

indicators.note: the word needs treatment, so its letters are worked over and rearranged

explanation.surface: A patient needs to be seen by a doctor in a German city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by' here means beside: the doctor's abbreviation stands next to the rearranged letters rather than performing the treatment.
explanation.definitionFit: The capital of the German state of Saxony, an example of a city there.
